name: Accessibility tree versus DOM versus screenshot versus markdown as an agent observation space. The comparison is not a single artifact but a design axis running through the web-agent literature. Named representations: AXTree (the browser-computed accessibility tree, reached via CDP Accessibility.getFullAXTree or Playwright's snapshot, and the default observation in BrowserGym/AgentLab, WebArena and WorkArena); raw DOM/HTML (innerHTML, outerHTML, getHTML); screenshot, usually augmented as Set-of-Mark (SoM) with bounding boxes and numeric IDs drawn over interactable elements as in VisualWebArena and WebVoyager; and markdown, produced by Turndown, Jina Reader, Crawl4AI, Firecrawl and the Playwright-MCP style tools. Reduction techniques layered on top: PageDigest, FocusAgent, LineRetriever, Region4Web, AgentOccam-style pruning. Pure-vision variants: SeeAct-V, which uses screenshots as the only environmental observation with a separate visual grounding model.
kind: Research result and a design axis, plus the browser features (accessibility tree, CDP) and libraries that instantiate each option. Not a single standard, benchmark or service; the AXTree end of it rests on the WAI-ARIA and HTML-AAM standards and on per-engine accessibility implementations.
maturity: Production consensus with an unsettled research frontier. The practical convergence since roughly 2024 is on AXTree-first observation with optional screenshot augmentation -- it is the default in BrowserGym/AgentLab, in WebArena and WorkArena, and in most commercial browser-agent tooling. Raw full-page HTML is effectively deprecated as an observation format on token grounds. Screenshot-only is a live research line (SeeAct-V, visual grounding models) rather than production practice. Markdown occupies a separate niche: it dominates READING pipelines (retrieval, ingestion, summarisation) and is largely absent from ACTING pipelines, because it drops the element identifiers an actuator needs. The observation-reduction sub-literature (PageDigest, FocusAgent, LineRetriever, Region4Web) is active and new, which is itself a signal that none of the four base representations is considered adequate as-is.
license: Nothing here is licence-blocked. The accessibility tree is a browser feature exposed by royalty-free standards. BrowserGym and AgentLab are open source (Apache-2.0-family). Turndown is MIT. The benchmarks (WebArena, VisualWebArena, WorkArena) are permissively licensed research artifacts. CDP is an open protocol. Commercial markdown serialisers have their own terms and are covered in item 4. [uncertain] on the exact licence of any individual reduction implementation the project might vendor.
keeps_and_discards: The four representations discard along four different axes and the differences are not a quality ordering. AXTREE keeps semantic ROLE, accessible NAME, and computed STATE for every element the accessibility engine considers relevant, and it keeps hierarchy. It discards presentational markup, most attributes, class names, ids that are not surfaced, raw text that is not an accessible name or content node, and -- critically -- everything the accessibility engine decides is not accessibility-relevant, including aria-hidden subtrees and elements the engine prunes. The accessible name is a COMPUTED value produced by the accessible-name-computation algorithm (aria-label, aria-labelledby, label element, alt, title, content, in a defined precedence), so what appears in an AXTree is the result of an algorithm, not the page's text. DOM/HTML keeps everything in the node tree and discards only what markup cannot express (form property state, canvas, CSSOM, generated content -- see item 26). SCREENSHOT keeps exactly what a human sees, including CSS generated content, canvas, video frames and rendered text in images, and discards everything not painted -- which means it is the ONLY representation that sees pseudo-element content and canvas, and the only one that cannot see hidden content. MARKDOWN keeps prose, headings, lists, links and tables and discards element identity, most interactivity, all state, and every structural distinction that has no markdown equivalent. The single most important asymmetry for this project: screenshot and AXTree both apply a visibility/relevance filter that the DOM and markdown do not, so a display:none injection is visible in DOM and markdown and INVISIBLE in a screenshot, and usually invisible in an AXTree because the accessibility engine prunes non-rendered content. That is a safety property the layout-blind representations structurally lack.
structure_preserved: AXTree preserves a hierarchy, but it is the ACCESSIBILITY hierarchy, not the DOM hierarchy: presentational wrappers are collapsed, roles restructure containment (a table's row/cell relations become explicit roles), and pruned subtrees vanish, so AXTree structure is a lossy semantic re-derivation and not recoverable back to DOM addresses without the browser's own bid/backendNodeId mapping. DOM preserves structure exactly, including shadow boundaries if getHTML options are used. Screenshot preserves only 2D geometry, and Set-of-Mark restores a flat list of identified elements with no hierarchy at all -- SoM is a set, as the name says, and reading nesting off a screenshot requires spatial inference. Markdown preserves a shallow reading order plus heading hierarchy and list nesting, loses table structure past simple grids, and loses shadow boundaries and element identity entirely. For a design keyed on url:xpath, the decisive point is that ONLY the DOM representation supplies stable, exact addresses; AXTree addresses are engine-internal identifiers that change across versions and are not xpaths, SoM ids are per-screenshot and ephemeral, and markdown has no addresses at all. Any representation the project emits must therefore carry its own address back-reference, because three of the four standard options destroy it.
interactive_elements: This is the axis on which the four separate most sharply. AXTree is designed around interactivity: every control has a role (button, textbox, checkbox, combobox, link), an accessible name, and a focusable/actionable indication, so 'what can I do here' is directly readable. DOM carries the same information but requires interpretation -- a div with a click handler and role=button looks like a div, and a semantic button looks like a button, and telling the two apart from markup alone requires exactly the tag-plus-interactivity inference the project intends to do. SoM screenshots make interactability explicit by construction: a JavaScript preprocessing pass finds interactable elements, draws bounding boxes and assigns numeric ids, so the model sees a labelled set of clickable things -- this is why VisualWebArena and WebVoyager both use it. Markdown loses controls almost completely: a button becomes text or disappears, a select becomes nothing, a form becomes a gap. That single fact is why markdown dominates reading pipelines and is nearly absent from acting pipelines, and it is the clearest statement of what a markdown-first fold must add back.
interactive_state_fidelity: The AXTree's decisive advantage and the reason it is not simply a worse DOM. It carries COMPUTED state -- checked, selected, expanded, disabled, pressed, current, invalid, required, level, posinset/setsize -- resolved from whichever of the attribute, the property, or the native control state actually applies. That resolution is exactly what markup cannot do: the DOM's checked ATTRIBUTE is the default and diverges from checkedness after any interaction, and getHTML serialises the attribute (item 26), so a DOM-based fold reports a filled form as empty while an AXTree reports it correctly. The token cost of this is low -- a few tokens per stateful control, emitted inline as part of the node line -- and this is the axis on which 'tag plus interactivity' has to earn its keep. The honest assessment for this project: tag plus interactivity derived from the DOM gets the AFFORDANCE right (this is clickable, this is a text field) and gets the STATE wrong wherever state is property-backed, unless the sensor reads the IDL properties directly. Reading input.value, .checked, .selected, .indeterminate and the ARIA-computed equivalents off live elements is cheap, requires no layout, and closes most of the gap -- it is a property read, not a geometry read, so it is legitimately inside the fold. Doing so is the single highest-value fidelity addition available and it is not a heuristic, because it reads declared state rather than inferring meaning. Screenshots convey state only as pixels, requiring the model to see a tick mark; markdown conveys none.
layout_awareness: Complete separation across the four, and this is where the project's no_layout_in_the_fold constraint sorts them. Screenshot IS layout -- it is nothing but geometry -- and Set-of-Mark is layout plus an id map, so both belong strictly in the actuator layer. AXTree is layout-DEPENDENT in a way that is easy to miss and important: the accessibility engine prunes elements that are not rendered, so producing an AXTree requires style resolution and the tree's CONTENTS depend on layout even though its output contains no coordinates. That makes AXTree a layout-derived artifact wearing textual clothing, which is a genuine constraint problem -- adopting the AXTree as the fold format would import a geometry dependency through the back door, invisibly. DOM and markdown are layout-free. The ASCII cartesian wireframe the project describes is unambiguously an actuator-side, geometry-consuming rendering and sits with the screenshot.
javascript_required: AXTree and screenshot both require a live, rendered page and therefore a browser with scripts run -- they cannot be produced from fetched bytes. DOM can be either (fetched HTML parsed offline, or live). Markdown can be produced from any of them. Consequence for telemetry: producing an AXTree or a screenshot means the page is live and its scripts are running, so analytics, beacons and third-party requests fire during observation; a fetch-and-parse markdown pipeline fires only the initial request. The project's in-page sensor is already in the live case, so this is not a new cost, but it does mean the choice of representation cannot be used to reduce telemetry exposure -- the exposure is set by the decision to render at all.
evaluation_method: Task success rate on interactive web benchmarks with programmatic checkers, ablating the observation space while holding the model and the agent loop fixed. BrowserGym/AgentLab is the standard harness for this: it supplies screenshot, HTML DOM and AXTree with a consistent element-metadata scheme (bid identifiers) so that the same agent can be run on any subset, with parallelised runs, failure recovery, and success rates reported with standard errors across episodes. This is a genuinely good methodology -- shared harness, consistent element ids across modalities, multiple episodes -- and it is the reason observation-space claims in this area are more trustworthy than extraction-quality claims elsewhere in this research set. Its limits: benchmark task sets are small and mostly simulated (WebArena's sites are self-hosted clones), success is binary per task so partial-fidelity differences are invisible, and the model is a confound that changes between papers.
corpus_size_and_origins: WebArena is 812 tasks over five self-hosted, cloned websites (a shopping site, a shopping admin, a forum, a code-hosting site and a map) plus wiki and calculator utilities -- so the ORIGIN COUNT IS FIVE, all simulated, all English, all frozen, and none of them is a real commercial page with real advertising, consent banners, third-party embeds or A/B tests. VisualWebArena adds 910 visually-grounded tasks over three of those environments. WorkArena is built on a live ServiceNow instance, so it is one enterprise application. This is the field's central reach problem and it is severe: an observation-space finding measured on five clean clones may not survive contact with a page carrying a cookie wall, four ad iframes and a chat widget, all of which inflate the DOM and the AXTree differently and inflate a screenshot not at all. The reduction papers (PageDigest, FocusAgent, LineRetriever) are evaluated on the same five environments. Nothing in this literature is measured on a corpus resembling 136 pages from 109 real origins, which means the project's own corpus is more origin-diverse than the entire web-agent observation literature and its measurements would be a genuine contribution rather than a replication.
reported_precision_recall: Task success rates and token counts, with denominators. TOKEN COST: PageDigest reduces observation length by 43% on average, from 6,437 to 3,671 tokens, and improves task success rate by 2.3 percentage points across four backbone models on WebArena -- this is the cleanest published number pair in the area because it reports both axes against the same control and shows reduction IMPROVING accuracy rather than trading against it. Widely circulated vendor-blog figures put an AXTree page at roughly 200-400 tokens against 15,000+ tokens for full DOM (about 93% reduction) and a screenshot at roughly 50,000 tokens; these are order-of-magnitude plausible and are NOT from a controlled study -- see evidence_independence. MODALITY EFFECT: in a direct comparison on a GoCalendar task set using Gemini 2.5 Flash, adding screenshots to AXTree observations did not significantly change attack success rate or benign utility (p>0.5, Fisher's exact test on both), i.e. the screenshot added nothing measurable on top of the AXTree for that task family. ABSOLUTE DIFFICULTY: baseline multimodal agents on VisualWebArena achieve about 16.4% success, with the authors attributing failures to OCR, spatial reasoning and contextual understanding -- a reminder that on visually-grounded tasks all representations are currently poor. Denominator caveats: all of these are five-environment, simulated-site numbers with per-paper model choices, and full-page HTML is frequently excluded from comparisons on the stated grounds that it is prohibitively large and exhausts context, which means the DOM arm of the comparison is often not measured at all rather than measured and found wanting.
independent_oracle: Yes for task success -- benchmark checkers verify final environment state programmatically (was the order placed, was the issue assigned) without sharing assumptions with the agent's perception, which is a real oracle. No for REPRESENTATION FIDELITY: nothing checks whether a given observation format actually preserved the page's content, only whether the agent succeeded at the task, and an agent can succeed on a task while the representation dropped most of the page. That is the gap this project's oracle-free metrics (item 9) and round-trip tests are aimed at, and it is genuinely unfilled here. A second-order oracle worth noting: cross-modality agreement -- if AXTree and DOM disagree about whether an element exists or what it says, one of them is wrong, and the disagreement rate is measurable without any gold standard.
evidence_independence: This field is unusually mixed and the mixture must be kept straight. The benchmark-based ablations (BrowserGym/AgentLab, PageDigest, FocusAgent, the AXTree-plus-screenshot comparison) are academic, use shared harnesses, and are not vendor-run; PageDigest's 43%/2.3pp figures and the Fisher's-exact screenshot null result are of this kind and are citable. The widely repeated token-efficiency figures -- '93% more token-efficient than raw DOM', '200-400 tokens per page', '50,000 tokens per screenshot', 'the industry is converging on the accessibility tree' -- circulate through SEO, agent-readiness and scraping-vendor blogs and are not traceable to a controlled measurement; they are plausible but they are marketing-adjacent and MUST NOT be laundered into the record as research findings. Note also that markdown-serialiser comparisons in this space are almost entirely vendor-run and mutually contradictory (item 4 covers this directly), so any claim that markdown beats or loses to AXTree on fidelity currently has no independent basis. The honest state: the ORDERING of token costs (AXTree < markdown < DOM << screenshot) is well established and uncontroversial; the specific ratios are not independently measured; and the accuracy consequences are measured only on five simulated sites.
page_archetype_coverage: Not broken out anywhere, and the mechanism predicts a large spread that the five-environment benchmarks cannot show. AXTree quality depends entirely on how well a page is authored for accessibility: a well-built application with semantic elements and correct ARIA produces an excellent AXTree, and a div-soup page with click handlers and no roles produces an AXTree of generic elements with no names, on which an agent is blind. That means AXTree performance correlates with page quality in a way DOM performance does not, and the benchmark sites -- clean open-source applications -- sit at the good end of that distribution. Documentation and article archetypes favour markdown, which loses almost nothing on prose. Listing and collection archetypes favour AXTree, which collapses repetitive markup into roles with names. Service and transactional archetypes favour AXTree decisively because of state fidelity. Product and media-heavy archetypes are where screenshots earn their cost, since content in images and canvas is invisible to every text representation. Any single 'AXTree is best' claim aggregates over this spread the way a single extraction F-score does.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Under-examined and materially different across the four. AXTree is the most locale-aware by construction -- accessible names come from the page's own text and ARIA labels, and the tree carries no tokenisation -- but role names and state keywords are emitted in English regardless of page language, so a Japanese page yields Japanese names inside English role scaffolding, which is a mixed-language artifact whose effect on a model is unmeasured. Screenshots depend on OCR when text is in images and OCR quality varies enormously by script, with CJK and Arabic markedly worse than Latin; VisualWebArena's authors already cite OCR as a top failure cause on English content. Markdown is script-neutral for content but its structural conventions are Latin-centric and RTL text inside markdown tables and lists renders and re-parses unpredictably. DOM is fully script-neutral. Token cost differs sharply by script too -- CJK text costs substantially more tokens per character under common BPE tokenisers -- so any token-budget number measured on English pages understates cost on CJK pages, and every figure quoted in this item was measured on English. That is a reach limit on the whole area and it is never stated.
leaks_outward: The representation determines what leaves the machine, and the four differ by an order of magnitude in how much. A screenshot discloses the entire visual state including anything incidentally on screen; an AXTree discloses names and states of everything the accessibility engine surfaces, including on authenticated pages the user's own name, account details and message contents; a DOM capture discloses everything; markdown discloses the prose. For a locally-run model none of this leaves the machine, which is the strongest argument for the project's local-embedder posture. For a hosted model the choice of representation is a data-transfer decision. One further leak specific to the AXTree and screenshot paths: producing them requires a live rendered page, so the page's own telemetry and its third-party embeds fire during observation and the origins learn a visit occurred.
mechanism_detectability: Materially different across the four and this is a decisive consideration the literature ignores entirely. SCREENSHOT capture through CDP is not page-observable directly, but Set-of-Mark preprocessing INJECTS bounding-box overlays into the page, which is a DOM mutation and is trivially visible to the page's own MutationObserver -- SoM is self-announcing, and any covert sensor must not use it. AXTREE extraction via CDP requires a debugger attachment; CDP usage has a known detection surface (Runtime.enable and related signals are the subject of an active detection/evasion arms race, covered separately in this research set), so AXTree-by-CDP is more detectable than a plain DOM read. AXTree computation itself is a browser-internal artifact and there is no page-visible signal that it was requested. DOM reading via getHTML or property access is not detectable at all (item 26). MARKDOWN derived from a DOM read inherits the DOM read's invisibility. So the detectability ordering is roughly: DOM/markdown (undetectable) < AXTree via internal APIs < AXTree via CDP < Set-of-Mark screenshot (self-announcing). A design that refuses attachShadow patching on detectability grounds should apply the same reasoning here, and it argues against SoM and against CDP-based observation for the read path even where they are more convenient.
countermeasures: For the reader: prefer non-mutating extraction (no SoM overlays, no injected markers); prefer in-page property reads over CDP where equivalent; serialise per subtree to flatten timing. For fidelity, the countermeasure against AXTree pruning is to cross-check against the DOM, since disagreement is informative. For the page defending itself, the relevant asymmetry is that a page can degrade its AXTree cheaply (remove ARIA, use divs) with real accessibility cost to human users, which most sites will not do -- so AXTree availability is protected by the page's own incentive to be usable, which is an unusually robust property.
measured_fidelity_cost: One clean measurement and a lot of unmeasured territory. CLEAN: PageDigest's 43% observation-length reduction (6,437 to 3,671 tokens) came with a 2.3 percentage point IMPROVEMENT in task success across four backbones on WebArena -- so that particular compression had negative cost, which is strong evidence that a large fraction of a naive observation is noise that actively harms performance. NULL RESULT: adding a screenshot on top of an AXTree changed neither attack success rate nor benign utility significantly (p>0.5, Fisher's exact, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GoCalendar), so the screenshot's substantial token cost bought nothing measurable in that setting. UNMEASURED: what AXTree pruning drops relative to the DOM, expressed as content rather than as task success; what markdown drops relative to the DOM in interactive affordances; and whether any of these hold on real commercial pages rather than the five clean benchmark clones. The project's own measured position -- a projection drawing 80.9% of a page's affordances against a capture holding 99.7% -- is exactly this missing measurement, computed on a more diverse corpus than anything published here.
gate_state_at_capture: Absent from every representation and from every benchmark. WebArena's sites are self-hosted clones with no consent banners, no paywalls and no CAPTCHAs, so the entire observation-space literature is measured in a gate-free world. On real pages the gate materially changes each representation differently: a consent overlay dominates a screenshot and a Set-of-Mark id list, appears prominently in an AXTree as a modal dialog with focus trapped inside it, appears as a subtree in the DOM, and may or may not appear in markdown depending on the extractor. So the same page in the same gate state produces observations that differ in how obviously gated they look, and none of them records the fact. Gate state must be captured out of band and attached, and the benchmark literature offers no precedent for doing so.
determinism: DOM and markdown-from-DOM are deterministic for a fixed tree. AXTree is deterministic within one browser build for a fixed rendered state, but it is a COMPUTED artifact -- accessible names come from a precedence algorithm, pruning depends on rendering, and the tree reflects style resolution -- so it is deterministic only in the sense that a function of a larger, less stable input is deterministic. Screenshots are the least deterministic: fonts, device pixel ratio, animation phase, lazy-loaded images and scroll position all change the pixels, and OCR over them adds a second stochastic stage. Set-of-Mark ids are assigned by a preprocessing pass and are not stable across loads. Markdown is deterministic per serialiser and differs across serialisers (item 3), so 'markdown' names a family of non-equivalent functions rather than a format.
determinism_across_versions: This is the AXTree's worst property and it is routinely conflated with run-to-run determinism. The accessibility tree is an ENGINE IMPLEMENTATION, not a specified serialisation: what gets pruned, how names are computed in edge cases, which roles are exposed, and what the tree looks like for a given widget all change across Chromium releases, and differ between Chromium, Gecko and WebKit. CDP's Accessibility domain is explicitly experimental and its output shape has changed across protocol revisions. So an AXTree-based capture is pinned to a browser build in a way a DOM capture is not, and cross-build comparison of AXTree captures is unsound without re-baselining. Screenshots drift with every rendering change, font update and OS version. DOM drifts only with parser changes, which are far rarer and better documented. Markdown drifts with serialiser version. Ranking by cross-version stability: DOM > markdown (per pinned serialiser) > AXTree > screenshot. For a project that needs stored artifacts to remain comparable over time, that ordering is a strong argument for a DOM-derived fold with AXTree-derived STATE read in as annotations rather than an AXTree-shaped fold.
reproducibility: Benchmark results are reproducible to an unusual degree for this research set -- WebArena and WorkArena environments are self-hosted and versioned, BrowserGym/AgentLab is open source with parallelised runs and standard errors, and trajectories can be replayed -- which is precisely why the five-environment reach limitation is worth the tradeoff those authors made. What is NOT reproducible is anything measured against the live web, and the same freeze-the-bytes conclusion applies as elsewhere. For the project: a DOM capture (getHTML string) is a reproducible artifact from which markdown can be recomputed at any time; an AXTree capture is reproducible only alongside its browser build; a screenshot is reproducible as pixels but not re-derivable.
failure_modes: Per representation. AXTREE: unnamed generic elements on badly authored pages, so controls appear as anonymous buttons the agent cannot distinguish; pruning that silently removes content the accessibility engine judged irrelevant; ARIA misuse by the page producing confidently wrong roles and names, which is worse than no information; and complete blindness to content in canvas or images without alt text. DOM: token blowout that exhausts context (the reason it is excluded from most comparisons outright); no state fidelity; and framework-generated class and attribute noise dominating the signal. SCREENSHOT: OCR errors, spatial-reasoning failures and contextual misreading -- explicitly the three causes VisualWebArena's authors give for the 16.4% baseline; enormous token cost; blindness to anything below the fold or behind a scroll container; and, with SoM, self-announcing DOM mutation. MARKDOWN: loss of controls and state, table mangling, no addresses, and serialiser-to-serialiser incompatibility. CROSS-CUTTING: every reduction technique introduces a new failure -- if the reducer drops the element the task needed, the agent cannot recover because it does not know something was dropped, which is the truncation-visibility problem again.
failure_visibility: Poor across all four and worst for the reduced formats. An AXTree with pruned content looks complete; a markdown conversion that dropped a form looks like a page without a form; a screenshot that missed below-the-fold content looks like the whole page; a reduced observation that discarded the needed element looks like an observation. None of the standard formats carries an elision marker. This is a direct, cheap, unexploited improvement: emit explicit markers for what was NOT included -- pruned subtrees, truncated lists, unreachable regions, controls whose state could not be read -- so that absence is distinguishable from emptiness. The ACI literature (item 27) already establishes that eliminating ambiguous silence measurably helps; nobody in the observation-space literature has applied that rule to elision.
scale_limits: Token cost is the binding constraint and it is superlinear in effect, not just in size: each observation is carried in a transcript across steps, so a large per-step observation multiplies across the trajectory. Approximate ordering per page from the available figures, with the vendor-sourced ones flagged: AXTree in the hundreds to low thousands of tokens (the 200-400 figure is vendor-sourced; PageDigest's measured WebArena baseline observation is 6,437 tokens, which is a controlled figure and an order of magnitude higher, and the discrepancy is itself worth noting -- 'AXTree' can mean a terse role/name listing or a full tree with attributes, and the two differ by 10x); markdown typically a few thousand for an article; full DOM commonly 15,000-100,000+ and routinely exhausting context; screenshot as image tokens in the tens of thousands. The practical wall is not one page but a trajectory of pages, and the reduction literature exists because the wall is hit at step three, not step one.
delta_cost_model: None of the four representations has one -- all are full re-observations of the current state, recomputed from scratch each step, which is the field's blind spot and the project's opportunity. Each step costs O(page) in the chosen representation regardless of how little changed, and no benchmark harness diffs observations between steps. What would fall outside a per-change cost if a delta model were built on each: for DOM/markdown, the exceptions are those of item 24 (shadow discovery, slot reassignment, CSS-driven change, canvas, form property state, declarative shadow DOM at parse) plus the O(subtree) cost of re-serialising an added subtree; for AXTREE, additionally the fact that the accessibility tree is recomputed by the engine from style and layout, so a CSS-only change with no DOM mutation can change the AXTree with no mutation record to signal it -- an exception that makes an O(delta) AXTree strictly harder than an O(delta) DOM; for SCREENSHOT, essentially everything, since any repaint changes pixels and there is no change signal short of comparing images. The ordering of how well each supports incrementality -- DOM > markdown > AXTree >> screenshot -- is the inverse of the token-cost ordering in one place and aligns with it in another, and it is a genuine argument for a DOM-based fold with AXTree state read as a per-node annotation rather than as the substrate.
reanchoring_stability: DOM addresses (xpath, or better, xpath plus content hash) are the only ones with any cross-load stability, and even they are fragile (item 23). AXTree node ids are engine-internal, change every load and every build, and are not addresses in any durable sense -- BrowserGym works around this by assigning its own bid identifiers consistently across modalities, which is a harness-level solution and exactly the right pattern: define your own address space and map every representation into it. Set-of-Mark ids are per-screenshot and meaningless across loads. Markdown has no addresses. The transferable design is BrowserGym's: one canonical element identity, assigned by the sensor, carried into every representation, so AXTree state, DOM structure and (in the actuator layer) screen geometry all key to the same address -- which is exactly what a trie keyed on url:xpath already provides, and it means the project's key can be the join column for all four representations rather than competing with them.
adversarial_exposure: The sharpest and most decision-relevant contrast in this item, and it cuts against the project's design. Screenshots and, largely, AXTrees are RENDERING-FILTERED: content that is display:none, zero-sized, off-screen or aria-hidden does not appear in a screenshot and is generally pruned from the accessibility tree, so both are structurally resistant to the concealment class that accounts for roughly 58.6% of concealed injections. DOM and markdown-from-DOM preserve all of it, so a layout-blind fold is strictly MORE exposed than the AXTree-based observation it would replace, and that must be stated plainly rather than argued around. What a layout-blind, DOM-based fold CAN address without geometry: (1) Unicode-level concealment -- tag characters, bidi controls, zero-width characters, homoglyphs -- entirely, because it is a property of the code points; (2) attribute-declared hiding -- the hidden attribute, aria-hidden, tabindex=-1, inert -- entirely, by reading attributes as strings; (3) inline-style-declared hiding -- reading 'display:none', 'visibility:hidden', 'opacity:0', tiny font sizes, absolute positioning off-canvas out of the style ATTRIBUTE as text, which is a string operation on DOM data, not a layout read, and is legitimately inside the fold; (4) semantic and structural anomalies -- a text node of instruction-shaped content inside a container with no other text, unusual density, mismatch between an element's accessible name and its text content. What it CANNOT address without geometry: stylesheet-driven concealment (a class whose rule lives in a stylesheet), computed-style concealment from cascade or media/container queries, clip-path and transform-based hiding, z-index occlusion, and anything requiring knowledge of what actually painted. Rough shape of the ceiling: the layout-free mechanisms cover all Unicode-level concealment and the attribute- and inline-style-declared portion of rendering-based concealment, which is a substantial but unquantified fraction of that 58.6% -- and the honest position is that the fraction is unmeasured, that it is the single most important number for this design's safety story, and that measuring it (classify each concealed injection in a real corpus by whether its concealment is expressed in the DOM or only in a stylesheet) is a tractable experiment nobody has run. Everything beyond that ceiling has to be handled by the actuator layer, which has geometry, or accepted as declared residual risk.
provenance_carrying: None of the four carries provenance natively. AXTree nodes have engine ids that map back to DOM nodes only through the browser's own tables; screenshots and SoM carry pixel positions; markdown carries nothing. The BrowserGym pattern of a harness-assigned identity present in every modality is the only working precedent and it exists to serve action targeting, not provenance. For this project the situation is inverted and favourable: the trie key already IS the provenance (url, xpath, shadow depth, capture time), so the design question is not how to obtain provenance but how to keep it attached through the projection -- a per-block or per-line address token, or an out-of-band offset map, both of which cost tokens or complexity and neither of which the literature has evaluated. Note that provenance the model cannot see cannot affect how the model treats the content, which argues for inline markers over side maps wherever injection resistance matters.
roundtrip_safety: Only the DOM representation round-trips (item 26: getHTML plus parseHTMLUnsafe is a designed fixed point). AXTree cannot be converted back into a page. A screenshot cannot. Markdown->HTML->markdown is a fixed point only for the subset of markdown the serialiser emits, and in practice is not one across serialisers. This asymmetry is a strong and under-used argument: the DOM is the only representation for which an oracle-free fidelity metric exists at all, and any pipeline that wants to make fidelity claims without a gold standard has to keep a DOM-shaped artifact somewhere. Escaping policy is a live hazard specifically for markdown, where page text containing markdown constructs alters the structure of the emitted document -- covered in item 15 -- and where the AXTree's plain-text names are comparatively safe because they are not being embedded in a structural syntax.
token_budget_and_ordering: The core design guidance this item exists to supply. (1) THE ORDERING OF COSTS is established: AXTree cheapest, markdown next, DOM an order of magnitude more, screenshot most expensive by far. The specific ratios are largely vendor-sourced and should not be quoted as measured; the one controlled datum is PageDigest's WebArena baseline of 6,437 tokens per observation reduced to 3,671. (2) REDUCTION CAN IMPROVE ACCURACY, NOT JUST COST: 43% fewer tokens with 2.3 percentage points BETTER success across four models is the clearest evidence in this research set that a naive observation contains actively harmful noise, and it means a budgeted projection should be treated as an accuracy intervention, not a concession. (3) SCREENSHOTS DID NOT ADD VALUE on top of an AXTree in a controlled test (p>0.5 on both utility and attack success), so the most expensive modality is not automatically the most informative -- an argument for keeping geometry out of the default read path that happens to align with the project's constraint. (4) WHAT TO EMIT AND IN WHAT ORDER: the evidence supports emitting a role/name/state-annotated structural skeleton first and content on demand, since that is what AXTree effectively is and what the reduction papers converge on. On position specifically, this literature is silent and item 30's findings must govern -- but the interaction is important: if attention becomes recency-dominant past roughly half the context fill, then a long observation placed early is worse than a short one placed late, which strengthens the case for aggressive per-step budgets in a multi-step trajectory rather than for one large well-organised dump. (5) A CONCRETE DEFAULT SHAPE for text(budget=...): emit the node's own content plus a COMPLETE child list with role/interactivity/state annotations and per-child size estimates, truncate by DEPTH rather than by document order so the frame is structurally complete at every level, mark every elision explicitly with what was elided and how much, and put the addresses inline. Complete-and-shallow beats partial-and-deep, because a model that knows what it has not seen can ask, and a model reading a truncated prefix cannot.
representation_cost: Per page, with sourcing flagged: AXTree hundreds to low thousands of tokens (vendor blogs say 200-400; the measured WebArena observation baseline is 6,437, and the discrepancy reflects that 'AXTree' covers both a terse role/name listing and a full annotated tree); markdown low thousands for an article; DOM 15,000 to 100,000+ and frequently context-exhausting; screenshot on the order of tens of thousands of image tokens, with a commonly cited but unsourced 50,000 figure. What is lost per token saved, by representation: AXTree saves by discarding presentational markup and non-accessible content, losing hidden-content visibility and exact addresses; markdown saves by discarding interactivity and state, losing the ability to act; screenshot spends heavily to gain rendered-only content (canvas, generated content, images) and visibility filtering. All figures are English-page figures and understate CJK cost.
what_could_be_adopted: Six things. (1) READ IDL STATE PROPERTIES AS PER-NODE ANNOTATIONS rather than adopting the AXTree as a format. Reading .value, .checked, .selected, .indeterminate, .disabled and the resolved ARIA state off live elements is a property read requiring no layout and no CDP, it closes the single largest fidelity gap between a DOM-derived fold and an AXTree, it costs a few tokens per stateful control, and it is not a heuristic because it reads declared state rather than inferring meaning. This is the highest-value item here. (2) THE BROWSERGYM IDENTITY PATTERN: one canonical element identity assigned by the sensor and carried into every representation, so DOM structure, state annotations and actuator-side geometry all key to the same address. The project's url:xpath key already is this; the point is to use it as the join column deliberately rather than letting each layer invent its own ids. (3) COMPLETE-CHILD-LIST-WITH-DEPTH-TRUNCATION as the budget shape, supported by the reduction papers' convergence and by the ACI evidence in item 27. (4) EXPLICIT ELISION MARKERS, which nothing in this literature does and which converts the universal silent-truncation failure into a visible one. (5) THE CROSS-MODALITY DISAGREEMENT ORACLE: where DOM and AXTree disagree about an element's existence, name or state, that disagreement is a free, gold-standard-free fidelity signal, and it is also a concealment signal -- content present in the DOM and pruned from the AXTree is, by definition, content the browser thinks is not rendered, which is a layout-derived hint obtainable without the fold ever touching geometry. That last observation deserves emphasis: the AXTree is a geometry-informed artifact with a text interface, so consulting it in the ACTUATOR layer as a concealment oracle is a way to get the visibility signal the fold cannot have, without putting geometry in the fold. (6) THE ABLATION METHODOLOGY, including reporting standard errors across episodes. Explicitly NOT to be adopted: Set-of-Mark preprocessing, which mutates the page and is self-announcing; CDP-based AXTree extraction in the read path, on detectability grounds; and the AXTree as the fold's substrate, on cross-version-instability and layout-dependence grounds.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: MIXED, AND THE AXTREE IS THE PROBLEM CASE. The accessibility tree assigns SEMANTIC ROLES -- navigation, main, article, banner, contentinfo, search -- which is precisely a classifier naming a region, and adopting AXTree roles as fold content would import exactly the pre-computed structural heuristic the constraint forbids. But the roles are AUTHOR-DECLARED rather than inferred, which is a real distinction: reading role=navigation off a page is reading an attribute the author wrote, the same as reading a class name, and it is not the sensor computing a judgement. VERDICT: author-declared role and state attributes are ADOPTABLE AS-IS as opaque tokens on the same footing as any other attribute, provided the fold does not ACT on their semantics (does not skip role=navigation, does not prioritise role=main); the accessibility engine's PRUNING and NAME-COMPUTATION decisions are engine-computed relevance judgements and are ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY or as an oracle, not as fold content. Relevance-based reduction methods (PageDigest, FocusAgent, LineRetriever, Region4Web) rank or select page regions by task relevance and are REJECTED as fold mechanisms, though their measured finding that reduction improves accuracy is adoptable as motivation for budget discipline. no_layout_in_the_fold: DOM and markdown ADOPTABLE AS-IS. AXTree is ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY -- it is layout-derived (pruning depends on rendering) even though its output contains no coordinates, and treating it as text-only would smuggle geometry into the fold invisibly; this is the item's most easily missed constraint violation. Screenshot and Set-of-Mark: ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY, unambiguously, alongside the ASCII wireframe. o_delta: ALL FOUR ARE NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY as practised -- every benchmark harness re-observes the full page every step and none diffs, so the literature demonstrates the cost of the non-incremental approach without offering a remedy. The transferable finding is the ordering of how well each COULD support incrementality (DOM > markdown > AXTree >> screenshot) and the specific exception that an AXTree can change from a CSS-only change with no mutation record, making an O(delta) AXTree strictly harder than an O(delta) DOM. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS methodologically -- real browsers, real rendering, programmatic state checkers -- with the caveat that the five self-hosted benchmark environments are simulated SITES, which is not a mocked measurement path but is a narrow and unusually clean corpus, so figures from it are NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY for real-web behaviour. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NOTABLE AND ADVERSE. The accessibility tree is computed by the browser over the composed tree INCLUDING closed shadow roots, so an AXTree exposes content that no DOM API will hand over -- which makes AXTree extraction a de-facto closed-root bypass. It does not patch attachShadow, so it does not violate the letter of the constraint, but it defeats its purpose, and a design that refuses attachShadow patching because closed means closed should treat AXTree-derived closed-root content the same way. VERDICT: REJECTED for reaching closed-root content; the constraint should be read as being about the boundary, not about the technique. OVERALL: read IDL state properties into a DOM-shaped fold; keep AXTree, screenshot and Set-of-Mark in the actuator layer; use AXTree-versus-DOM disagreement as an oracle rather than as content; reject relevance-based reduction and reject AXTree as a closed-root workaround.
governance_signal_handling: None of the four representations engages with robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt, AIPREF, Web Bot Auth or HTTP 402 -- all are in-page reads after retrieval, and the benchmarks run against self-hosted environments where no governance signal exists. Two second-order points. First, an agent that navigates autonomously performs retrievals whose governance was never checked, and the observation layer gives no hook for checking; governance must sit at the navigation layer. Second, there is an emerging and awkward interaction worth flagging: because AXTree quality determines how well agents can use a site, a body of 'agent readiness' and 'accessibility-tree SEO' advice has appeared urging sites to optimise their accessibility trees FOR agents. That is a governance signal of a sort -- sites choosing to be legible to automation -- but it is informal, unstandardised, and pulls in the opposite direction from Content Signals-style opt-outs. Neither is represented in any observation format.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The representation choice is a data-minimisation choice and should be treated as one. A screenshot is the most exposing artifact possible -- it captures everything visible including material incidental to the task, and on an authenticated page that includes account identifiers, message content and anything else on screen. An AXTree captures names and states, which on an authenticated page includes the user's own name and personal fields, and notably includes the CURRENT VALUES of form controls, which markup-based capture does not. A DOM capture excludes typed form values by default (item 26), which makes it the more minimising choice for the most sensitive data category. Markdown is the least exposing and the least useful. So there is a genuine, non-obvious ordering here: DOM-plus-selective-state-reads is more privacy-preserving than an AXTree, because the AXTree hands over every field's current value indiscriminately while selective property reads are a deliberate, auditable choice per control. That argues for reading state properties on the controls the fold actually needs rather than adopting a format that carries all of them. Retention, erasure and lawful basis attach to whichever artifact is stored, keyed by the address scheme. [uncertain] on the specific lawful-basis analysis under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, which is item 19's subject.
